english_translation: Good evening, Mother. Today I am tired, but things went well nonetheless.

dialogue.shona: Manheru amai. Nhasi ndakaneta asi zvinhu zvafamba zvakanaka hazvo.
dialogue.english: Good evening, Mother. Today I am tired, but things went well nonetheless.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Manheru [good evening / evening] • amai [mother] • Nhasi [today] • ndakaneta [I (past) neta] • asi [but / however] • zvinhu [things nhu] • zvafamba [zvafamba] • zvakanaka [well / nicely / very good] • hazvo [hazvo]

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('Manheru')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'Manheru'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('ndakaneta')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'ndakaneta' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvakanaka'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: Evening Check-Ins with Mother ('Manheru Amai') After Work
cultural_notes.content: Returning home in the evening begins with a respectful greeting to one's parents ('Manheru amai') and a reassuring report on the day's work: even when tired ('ndakaneta'), adding 'zvinhu zvafamba zvakanaka hazvo' ('things went well nonetheless') expresses gratitude and resilience.

active_exercises.prompt: If a friend asks you in the afternoon 'Waswera sei?', what is the natural reply?
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, you reply to 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?') with 'Ndaswera kana waswerawo' ('I spent the day well if you spent it well too').

active_exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Mhoro' and 'Mhoroi'?
options: 'Mhoro' is for one peer/child, while 'Mhoroi' is for an elder or a group of people
'Mhoro' is used only at night, while 'Mhoroi' is used in the morning
'Mhoro' is used in shops, while 'Mhoroi' is used only at school
active_exercises.correct_answer: 'Mhoro' is for one peer/child, while 'Mhoroi' is for an elder or a group of people
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' ('Mhoro' -> 'Mhoroi') shows plural or respectful address.
